description.narrative:
Norad to maintain the 6.8M NOK over three years for each country office to carry out their activities. That means 2.27M NOK per year per country office. This funding to Ghana, Uganda and Kenya (20.4M NOK in total for the three countries) constitutes the bulk of the funds we are asking for and reflects a theory of change which is grounded in national work. Norad does not have a budget templatethat we need to use, and we are still looking at developing the overall budget for this call. As the project willlook fairly similar to the Fair Recovery project, I would ask that you develop a budget using the same budget lines as are used in the Fair Recovery project.
In the application, we will have quite limited space to describe the programme. Attached is adocument we have worked on which uses up the full word limit to describe the programme and the budget. Please have a look at it and send us back any comments you may have. Note that we are at full word limit, so we cannot add new sentences or paragraphs without removing something else, so please suggest changes in the text rather than adding new sentences. We will have opportunities in other parts of the application such as the detailed budget and the results framework to specify national partners and their activities.
Regarding country specific discussions, I was encouraged when we had our last conversation that you liked the FFD and Inequality framings, and that you were positive to the approach of strengthening the democratic dialogue and doing work in coalitions and actively supporting coalitions where possible. As has been discussed previously, this call for applications is highly competitive and we do need to speak to what Norad is asking of us. That is why we are stressing the need for all partners to devote some of their capacity towards wealth taxes and taxingHNWIs. This will look slightly different in different countries and contexts, but in order for us to present a coherent programme, we do request that all countries plan some activities - including national level advocacy - around these issues. There will be policy work within the project and the Oxfam confederation that OiU can draw on when crafting recommendations and advocacy work around this, including the Africa Inequality report. Note that we will also work with ATAF in the new project, a co-operation which opens up for exciting opportunities to do technical work the government on how to best set up policies and structures for taxing HNWIs. This should ideally be matched with resources from within each country office to build public support for more progressive taxation and proactive dialogue and advocacy with decision-makers on these issues.
Beyond the work on wealth taxation and taxing HNWIs that we hope that countries will engage in and also work together and learn from each other on, there will obviously be contextually relevant work in each country and we note the wish from OiU to also work on debt and on IFIs which can be accommodated within the overall narrative of the project as unsustainable debt directly impacts the ability of states to implement progressive budgets and spending on quality public services. We are a bit worried about too much fragmentation of policy focus though, and want to understand your suggested approaches to taxing the informal sector and trade taxes and whether that can fit into this programme. I know there is already a dialogue with Christian on this so I won't go into detail here, but it seems quite urgent to clarify those issues so please do letus know about your suggested approaches and how it can fit into the programme in a seamless way.
Regarding the work with journalists, I saw your comment on the draft overall narrative Sophie about whether we should focus more on capacity building oronsupporting journalists with actual stories. The capacity building reference is mainly for Finance Uncovered, while countries may be better off focusing on working with journalists on specific stories. Note that Finance Uncovered is hoping to provide moresupport to project countries on the work with journalists in the upcoming project.

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam Novib is one of the 17 national affiliates of the Oxfam International Confederation. It started life in 1956 as the Netherlands Organisation for International Assistance (Novib), and joined forces with Oxfam in 1994. Working together in confederation, the Oxfam affiliates can speak with one clear and compelling voice on issues of global concern: climate change, health and education forall, agriculture, trade, and conflicts and emergencies. Oxfam established this country office to support local organizations and projects. Through this local office Oxfam Novib directly contributes towards this project’s implementation.
